metadata.title: Core Terraform Concepts — Decision Intelligence Knowledge Base
metadata.description: Structured reasoning entries for Terraform core concepts. Used by AI Infrastructure Agent to make architecture decisions.

entries.description: Providers are plugins that allow Terraform to interact with cloud platforms, SaaS services, and APIs. Each provider exposes a set of resource types and data sources. For AWS, the hashicorp/aws provider is the authoritative interface to all AWS services. Provider version pinning is critical in production to prevent unintended drift from upstream API changes.
decision_rules: ALWAYS pin provider versions using ~> (pessimistic constraint) to allow only patch upgrades — e.g., ~> 5.0 locks to 5.x but not 6.0
USE multiple provider aliases when managing resources across different AWS regions or accounts in the same root module
DECLARE provider requirements in a dedicated versions.tf or providers.tf — never inline in main.tf
USE the aws provider alias pattern for cross-region resources like Route53, CloudFront (us-east-1), and disaster recovery replicas
UPGRADE provider versions deliberately and in isolation — never upgrade providers mid-feature development
tradeoffs: Pinning versions: stability and reproducibility vs. missing new resource types or security patches
Multi-provider configs: enables cross-account automation but increases complexity and auth surface
Frequent upgrades: access to new AWS services vs. risk of breaking changes in resource schemas
anti_patterns: Leaving provider version unconstrained (no version = latest = breaking changes on every plan)
Hardcoding AWS credentials inside the provider block — always use IAM roles or environment variables
Using the same provider for both DR regions without explicit aliases — causes plan conflicts
Mixing provider versions across modules without constraint alignment — leads to version conflicts
aws_alignment: Security Pillar: credential management through IAM roles, not static keys
Operational Excellence: version pinning enables reproducible deployments

entries.description: Resources are the fundamental building blocks of Terraform infrastructure. Each resource block maps to one real-world infrastructure object. Resource lifecycle, dependencies, and ordering are managed by Terraform's dependency graph. Understanding implicit vs. explicit dependencies and lifecycle hooks (create_before_destroy, prevent_destroy, ignore_changes) is critical for production-grade infrastructure.
decision_rules: USE implicit dependencies (reference expressions) over explicit depends_on — Terraform resolves them more efficiently
USE depends_on ONLY when a dependency exists that Terraform cannot detect through references (e.g., IAM policy propagation timing)
APPLY create_before_destroy lifecycle rule for resources that cannot have downtime during replacement (e.g., Auto Scaling Launch Templates, TLS certificates)
APPLY prevent_destroy to stateful resources: RDS instances, S3 buckets with data, EFS volumes
USE ignore_changes for attributes managed outside Terraform (e.g., AMI IDs managed by autoscaling, tags set by AWS Config)
tradeoffs: Granular resources: full control and visibility vs. more code and higher state complexity
Using AWS modules vs. raw resources: faster development vs. less control over individual settings
Lifecycle rules: prevents accidental deletion vs. may require manual intervention for replacements
anti_patterns: Creating resources without tagging — violates cost attribution and compliance requirements
Hardcoding resource names with no randomness suffix when a resource must be unique — causes naming conflicts on recreation
Not using count or for_each for repeated patterns — leads to copy-paste IaC with drift risk
Importing existing resources without a plan to bring them fully under Terraform management
aws_alignment: Operational Excellence: lifecycle rules prevent unintended downtime
Reliability: prevent_destroy on stateful resources reduces blast radius of accidents
Cost Optimization: tagging strategy enables cost allocation per team/environment

entries.description: Modules are reusable, composable units of Terraform configuration. They encapsulate related resources with a defined interface (input variables and outputs). Modules enforce consistency across environments and teams. There are two categories: root modules (what you execute) and child modules (what you call). The terraform-aws-modules GitHub organization provides battle-tested, AWS-specific modules like terraform-aws-modules/eks/aws that embed production defaults.
decision_rules: CREATE a module when the same infrastructure pattern repeats across 2+ environments or teams
USE public registry modules (terraform-aws-modules) for foundational patterns: VPC, EKS, RDS — they embed AWS best practices
BUILD internal modules for business-specific patterns: application stacks, compliance baselines
COMPOSE modules from smaller modules rather than monolithic super-modules — easier to test and maintain
VERSION pin all module sources — both registry modules (~> 20.0) and Git sources (?ref=v2.1.0)
EXPOSE only the variables that callers need to change — default all production-safe values inside the module
tradeoffs: Module abstraction: reduced duplication vs. abstraction cost — debugging requires understanding multiple layers
Public registry modules: fast adoption of best practices vs. opinionated defaults may not fit all use cases
Deep module nesting: clean separation vs. difficult to trace resource origins in plans
Module versioning: stability guarantee vs. delayed adoption of upstream security fixes
anti_patterns: Creating a single God-module that contains all infrastructure — untestable, unmaintainable, prevents independent deployments
Calling modules without pinned versions — upstream changes break your infrastructure on next init
Exposing every resource attribute as a module variable — creates a passthrough module with no value
Mixing module outputs with direct resource references in the same root module — creates unclear ownership
Duplicating AWS modules from public registry internally without adding value — maintenance burden with no benefit
aws_alignment: Operational Excellence: modules enforce standards across teams, reduce human error
Security Pillar: security baselines encoded in modules cannot be bypassed per-deployment
Cost Optimization: standardized modules prevent over-provisioned outliers

entries.description: Terraform state is the source of truth for managed infrastructure. In production, state must be stored remotely (S3) with encryption, versioning, and distributed locking (DynamoDB). State isolation between environments prevents a failed prod deployment from corrupting staging state. State should be organized by the blast radius of change — network state separate from application state.
decision_rules: ALWAYS use remote S3 backend in production — local state is a single point of failure and a security risk
ENABLE S3 versioning on the state bucket — enables rollback to previous known-good state
ENABLE S3 server-side encryption (AES-256 or KMS) for state at rest — state contains sensitive values
CREATE a DynamoDB table for state locking — prevents concurrent applies from corrupting state
SEPARATE state files by: environment (dev/staging/prod) AND layer (network, compute, data) — limits blast radius
USE terraform_remote_state data source to share outputs across state files rather than duplicating resources
RESTRICT S3 state bucket access via IAM — only CI/CD roles and authorized engineers should read/write
tradeoffs: State isolation by layer: small blast radius vs. more state files to manage and coordinate
Single monolithic state: simple coordination vs. any failure/lock blocks all deployments
KMS encryption: strong security vs. additional cost and KMS API dependency
State locking: prevents corruption vs. a crashed apply holds the lock until DynamoDB TTL expires
anti_patterns: Committing state files to Git — exposes secrets and resource IDs, creates merge conflicts
Using a single state file for all environments — a plan mistake in prod destroys the ability to manage dev
Not enabling state versioning — no recovery path after accidental terraform destroy
Sharing state files across teams with different deployment cadences — constant lock contention
Storing the state bucket and lock table in the same account as the managed infrastructure without separate access control
aws_alignment: Security Pillar: encrypted state, least-privilege access to state bucket
Reliability Pillar: state versioning enables recovery from accidental destruction
Operational Excellence: state isolation by layer enables independent team deployments

entries.description: Variables define the interface of a Terraform configuration, allowing reuse across environments. Outputs expose resource attributes for consumption by other modules or root configurations. A disciplined variable strategy separates environment-specific values (tfvars files) from module defaults, and sensitive values from non-sensitive ones. Outputs should expose exactly what downstream consumers need — not raw resource objects.
decision_rules: DECLARE variable types explicitly — prevents runtime errors from type mismatches
MARK variables as sensitive = true for passwords, tokens, and private keys — prevents Terraform from printing them in logs
USE .tfvars files per environment (dev.tfvars, prod.tfvars) — never commit prod values to Git
SET safe default values for optional variables, requiring only what must differ per environment
OUTPUT the minimum surface area: IDs, ARNs, DNS names — not full resource objects
USE output descriptions — downstream teams and modules need to know what an output represents
VALIDATE variables with custom validation blocks when the range of valid values is constrained
tradeoffs: Strict typing: catches errors early vs. requires more upfront definition work
Sensitive marking: protects secrets in logs vs. makes debugging harder when values are hidden
Many fine-grained variables: highly flexible module interface vs. complex caller experience
Defaulting everything: fast to call vs. hides important configuration that should be intentional
anti_patterns: Passing secrets as plain-text variables in tfvars committed to version control
Using string type for all variables — loses validation and readability benefits
Outputting entire resource objects — exposes unintended attributes and creates tight coupling
Not validating list or map variable lengths when the module expects specific counts
Using variable names that shadow Terraform built-in functions or keywords
aws_alignment: Security Pillar: sensitive variables prevent credential leakage in CI/CD logs
Operational Excellence: typed and validated variables reduce deployment errors

entries.description: Data sources allow Terraform to read existing infrastructure state without managing it. They are the bridge between Terraform-managed resources and pre-existing AWS resources (shared VPCs, AMIs, account IDs, Route53 zones). Correct use of data sources prevents hardcoding IDs and ARNs, making configurations portable across accounts and regions.
decision_rules: USE aws_caller_identity data source to get the current account ID dynamically — never hardcode account IDs
USE aws_availability_zones data source to enumerate AZs — prevents hardcoded AZ names that differ by region
USE aws_ami data source to find the latest approved AMI — ensures patched images without manual updates
USE aws_vpc or aws_subnet data sources when referencing shared network infrastructure not managed by this root module
USE aws_ssm_parameter data source to fetch secrets at plan time — keeps secrets out of tfvars
tradeoffs: Data sources vs. hardcoded values: portability and freshness vs. plan time API calls that can fail
Dynamic AMI lookup: always latest vs. unpredictable changes to instance startup behavior
Remote state data source vs. direct data source: explicit dependency graph vs. tight coupling between state files
anti_patterns: Hardcoding AMI IDs — becomes outdated immediately, breaks in other regions
Hardcoding account IDs — module is not portable across accounts
Using data sources to read resources managed by the same root module — creates circular dependencies
Not filtering data sources sufficiently — returns unexpected resources in complex accounts
aws_alignment: Operational Excellence: dynamic references prevent configuration drift from manual changes
Reliability: latest AMI data source ensures patched base images

entries.concept: Terraform Workspaces vs. Directory-Based Environment Isolation
entries.description: Terraform offers two strategies for environment isolation: workspaces (logical separation within the same backend) and directory-based isolation (separate root modules per environment). Workspaces are a common source of production incidents because they share a codebase and can be accidentally targeted. Directory-based isolation is the AWS and HashiCorp recommended approach for prod/staging/dev separation.
decision_rules: USE directory-based isolation (separate root modules) for production environments — dev/, staging/, prod/ each have their own state
USE workspaces ONLY for ephemeral, identical environments like PR preview environments or feature branch testing
NEVER use workspaces to separate prod from staging — the risk of running plan/apply in the wrong workspace is too high
STRUCTURE directories to mirror environment blast radius: changes to prod/ require explicit directory targeting
tradeoffs: Workspaces: DRY code vs. implicit environment selection — easy to apply to wrong environment
Directory isolation: explicit and safe vs. code duplication across environment directories (mitigated by shared modules)
Workspace approach: single codebase vs. single backend failure affects all environments
anti_patterns: Using workspaces for prod/staging/dev differentiation in critical systems
Not validating current workspace before destructive operations in CI/CD
Allowing workspace switching without MFA or approval gates in production pipelines
aws_alignment: Reliability Pillar: directory isolation prevents blast radius cross-contamination between environments
Security Pillar: explicit environment targeting reduces risk of accidental production changes
